title: UNIT 3: CELL BIOLOGY
notes:
✓ The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life.

Cells have specialized structures that perform specific functions, exchange materials with their environment and form higher levels of biological organization.

title: 3.2 Cell Theory
notes:
✓ Cell theory states that:
◆ All living organisms are made of one or more cells.
◆ The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life.
◆ All cells arise from pre-existing cells.
◆ Cells contain hereditary information that is passed to new cells.

title: 3.3 Cell Structure and Function
notes:
Cells contain structures called organelles that perform specific functions.

◆ Cell membrane → controls movement of substances in and out.
◆ Cytoplasm → site of many chemical reactions.
◆ Nucleus → contains DNA and controls cell activities.
◆ Mitochondria → produce ATP through cellular respiration.
◆ Ribosomes → synthesize proteins.
◆ Endoplasmic reticulum → synthesizes and transports proteins and lipids.
◆ Golgi apparatus → modifies, packages and transports substances.
◆ Lysosomes → digest waste and cellular materials.
◆ Vacuole → stores water, nutrients and wastes.
◆ Chloroplast → carries out photosynthesis in plant cells.

title: 3.4 Types of Cells
notes:
Cells are broadly classified into two types:

PROKARYOTIC CELLS:
◆ Usually smaller and simpler.
◆ No true nucleus.
◆ DNA is located in a nucleoid region.
◆ Lack membrane-bound organelles.
◆ Example → bacteria.

EUKARYOTIC CELLS:
◆ Usually larger and more complex.
◆ Have a true nucleus.
◆ Contain membrane-bound organelles.
◆ Examples → plant, animal, fungal and protist cells.

title: 3.3.1 Cell Wall
notes:
✓ The cell wall is a rigid outer layer found in plant cells, fungi and many microorganisms.

Functions:
◆ Provides support and protection.
◆ Maintains cell shape.
◆ Prevents excessive water uptake and bursting.

→ Plant cell walls are mainly made of cellulose.

title: 3.3.2 Cell Membrane
notes:
✓ The cell membrane is a thin, flexible, selectively permeable boundary surrounding the cell.

Functions:
◆ Controls movement of substances into and out of the cell.
◆ Helps maintain internal conditions.
◆ Contains proteins involved in transport, communication and recognition.

→ It is mainly composed of phospholipids and proteins.

title: 3.3.3 Cytoplasm
notes:
✓ Cytoplasm is the region inside the cell membrane containing the cytosol and organelles, excluding the nucleus in eukaryotic cells.

Functions:
◆ Site of many metabolic reactions.
◆ Suspends and supports organelles.
◆ Allows movement of substances within the cell.

title: 3.3.4 Nucleus
notes:
✓ The nucleus is a membrane-bound organelle that contains most of the cell's DNA.

Functions:
◆ Controls many cell activities through gene expression.
◆ Stores genetic information.
◆ Coordinates cell growth and reproduction.

→ The nucleolus inside the nucleus produces rRNA and assembles ribosomal subunits.

title: 3.3.5 Ribosome
notes:
✓ Ribosomes are small structures made of rRNA and proteins that synthesize proteins.

They may be:
◆ Free in the cytoplasm → produce proteins mainly used inside the cell.
◆ Attached to rough ER → produce proteins for secretion, membranes or certain organelles.

→ Ribosomes occur in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.

title: 3.3.6 Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER)
notes:
✓ The endoplasmic reticulum is a membrane network involved in the production, processing and transport of substances within the cell.

Two main types:
◆ Rough ER.
◆ Smooth ER.

title: 3.3.7 Rough Endoplasmic Reticulum (RER)
notes:
✓ Rough ER has ribosomes attached to its surface, giving it a rough appearance.

Functions:
◆ Synthesizes proteins destined for secretion, membranes and certain organelles.
◆ Begins protein folding and modification.
◆ Transports proteins to the Golgi apparatus through vesicles.

title: 3.3.8 Smooth Endoplasmic Reticulum (SER)
notes:
✓ Smooth ER lacks ribosomes on its surface.

Functions:
◆ Synthesizes lipids and some hormones.
◆ Helps detoxify harmful substances.
◆ Stores and releases calcium ions in specialized cells.
◆ Participates in carbohydrate metabolism.

title: 3.3.9 Vesicles
notes:
✓ Vesicles are small membrane-bound sacs that transport or store substances inside cells.

Functions:
◆ Transport proteins and lipids between organelles.
◆ Carry materials to and from the cell membrane.
◆ Participate in endocytosis and exocytosis.

title: 3.3.10 Golgi Apparatus
notes:
✓ The Golgi apparatus, also called Golgi body or Golgi complex, is a stack of flattened membrane sacs.

Functions:
◆ Modifies proteins and lipids received from the ER.
◆ Sorts and packages substances into vesicles.
◆ Helps form lysosomes.
◆ Produces materials for secretion and cell membranes.

title: 3.3.11 Mitochondria
notes:
✓ Mitochondria are membrane-bound organelles that produce most of the cell's ATP through aerobic cellular respiration.

Features:
◆ Double membrane.
◆ Inner membrane forms folds called cristae.
◆ Matrix contains enzymes, mitochondrial DNA and ribosomes.

Often called the 'powerhouse' of the cell.

title: 3.3.12 Lysosomes
notes:
✓ Lysosomes are membrane-bound organelles containing digestive enzymes.

Functions:
◆ Break down worn-out cell components.
◆ Digest foreign materials and some cellular waste.
◆ Recycle useful cellular materials.

→ They are especially common in animal cells.

title: 3.3.13 Vacuoles
notes:
✓ Vacuoles are membrane-bound sacs used mainly for storage.

Functions:
◆ Store water, nutrients, pigments and wastes.
◆ In plant cells, the large central vacuole maintains turgor pressure and helps support the cell.

→ Plant cells usually have a large central vacuole, while animal cells may have smaller vacuoles.

title: 3.3.14 Chloroplasts
notes:
✓ Chloroplasts are photosynthetic organelles found mainly in plant cells and algae.

Functions:
◆ Carry out photosynthesis.
◆ Convert light energy into chemical energy stored in carbohydrates.

Features:
◆ Double membrane.
◆ Thylakoid membranes arranged into grana.
◆ Stroma contains enzymes, DNA and ribosomes.

title: 3.3.15 Centrioles and Microtubules
notes:
✓ Centrioles are cylindrical structures made of microtubules, commonly found in animal cells as part of the centrosome.

Functions:
◆ Help organize microtubules.
◆ Participate in formation of the spindle during cell division.
◆ Help organize structures such as cilia and flagella.

→ Microtubules are components of the cytoskeleton that help maintain cell shape and transport materials inside cells.

title: 3.3.16 Cilia and Flagella
notes:
✓ Cilia and flagella are hair-like structures containing microtubules that help cells or substances move.

Cilia:
◆ Usually short and numerous.
◆ Move substances across the cell surface or help move the cell.

Flagella:
◆ Usually longer and fewer.
◆ Commonly propel cells through liquid.

Example → sperm cells use a flagellum for movement.

title: 3.5 Animal and Plant Cells
notes:
✓ Both plant and animal cells are eukaryotic and contain a cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, ER and Golgi apparatus.

PLANT CELLS:
◆ Cell wall → support and protection.
◆ Chloroplasts → photosynthesis.
◆ Large central vacuole → storage and maintains turgor.
◆ Usually have a more fixed shape.

ANIMAL CELLS:
◆ No cell wall.
◆ No chloroplasts.
◆ Usually have smaller vacuoles.
◆ Often have a flexible or irregular shape.

title: 3.6 Observing Cells Under a Microscope
notes:
✓ Microscopes allow cells and their structures to be observed by magnification and resolution.

Basic procedure:
1. Prepare a thin specimen on a slide.
2. Add a suitable stain when necessary.
3. Place the slide on the stage.
4. Start with the lowest-power objective.
5. Focus using the coarse adjustment.
6. Use fine adjustment for a clear image.
7. Increase magnification when needed.

Total magnification = Eyepiece × Objective.

title: 3.7 The Cell and Its Environment
notes:
✓ The cell membrane separates the cell from its environment and regulates the movement of substances across it.

The membrane is selectively permeable, allowing some substances to pass while restricting others.

Transport across membranes may be passive or active.

title: 3.7.1 Passive Transport
notes:
✓ Passive transport is the movement of substances across a cell membrane without using cellular energy (ATP). Substances move down their concentration or electrochemical gradient.

Types:
◆ Simple diffusion → movement from high to low concentration.
◆ Facilitated diffusion → movement through membrane proteins from high to low concentration.
◆ Osmosis → movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane from higher water potential to lower water potential.

title: 3.7.1.1 Osmosis
notes:
✓ Osmosis is the net movement of water through a selectively permeable membrane toward the side with lower water potential.

Effects on cells:
◆ Hypotonic solution → water enters the cell.
◆ Hypertonic solution → water leaves the cell.
◆ Isotonic solution → no net movement of water.

Plant cells become turgid in hypotonic solutions and plasmolyzed in strongly hypertonic solutions.

title: 3.7.2 Active Transport
notes:
✓ Active transport moves substances across a membrane against their concentration or electrochemical gradient and requires energy, usually from ATP.

It uses specific transport proteins.

Examples:
◆ Sodium-potassium pump.
◆ Mineral ion uptake by plant root cells.

Bulk transport also requires energy:
◆ Endocytosis → substances enter the cell.
◆ Exocytosis → substances leave the cell.

title: 3.7.3 Passive vs Active Transport
notes:
PASSIVE TRANSPORT:
◆ Does not directly require ATP.
◆ Moves substances down their gradient.
◆ Includes diffusion, facilitated diffusion and osmosis.

ACTIVE TRANSPORT:
◆ Requires cellular energy.
◆ Moves substances against their gradient.
◆ Uses transport proteins or vesicles.

REMEMBER:
Passive → down the gradient, no ATP.
Active → against the gradient, requires energy.

title: 3.8 Levels of Biological Organization
notes:
✓ Biological organization proceeds from simple to complex:

Atom → Molecule → Organelle → Cell → Tissue → Organ → Organ system → Organism → Population → Community → Ecosystem → Biosphere.

◆ Cell → basic unit of life.
◆ Tissue → group of similar cells performing a function.
◆ Organ → different tissues working together.
◆ Organ system → organs working together.
◆ Organism → individual living thing.
◆ Population → members of one species in an area.
◆ Community → different populations living together.
◆ Ecosystem → community plus its physical environment.

title: UNIT 3 — MUST REMEMBER
notes:
Cell membrane → controls movement of substances.
Cell wall → support and protection.
Cytoplasm → site of many metabolic reactions.
Nucleus → DNA and control center.
Ribosome → protein synthesis.
Rough ER → protein synthesis and processing.
Smooth ER → lipid synthesis and detoxification.
Vesicles → transport and storage.
Golgi → modifies, sorts and packages substances.
Mitochondria → ATP production.
Lysosomes → intracellular digestion and recycling.
Vacuoles → storage; plant central vacuole maintains turgor.
Chloroplasts → photosynthesis.
Centrioles → microtubule organization and cell division.
Cilia → short, numerous movement structures.
Flagella → longer structures for cell movement.

Passive transport → no direct ATP, down gradient.
Active transport → energy required, against gradient.

EXAM TIP:
Rough ER = ribosomes + proteins.
Smooth ER = lipids + detoxification.
Golgi = modify + sort + package.
Mitochondria = ATP.
Chloroplast = photosynthesis.
